text: The Federal Meat Inspection Act of 1906 (FMIA) is an American law that prohibits the adulteration or misbranding of meat and meat products sold as food and ensures that such products are slaughtered and processed under strictly regulated sanitary conditions. These requirements extend to imported meat products, which must be inspected under equivalent foreign standards. USDA inspection of poultry was added by the Poultry Products Inspection Act of 1957 (PPIA). The Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act authorizes the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to provide inspection services for all livestock and poultry species not covered by the FMIA or PPIA, including venison and buffalo. The Agricultural Marketing Act authorizes the USDA to offer voluntary, fee-for-service inspection services for these same species. The original 1906 Act granted the Secretary of Agriculture the authority to inspect and condemn any meat product found unfit for human consumption. Unlike earlier laws aimed at preventing European nations from banning pork trade, this law was primarily driven by a desire to protect the American diet. All food labels had to be accurate, though not all ingredients were required to be listed. Although harmful food was banned, many warnings were still provided on containers. The production date for canned meats was included in the legislation introduced by Senator Albert Beveridge but was later removed in the House bill that became law. The law was partly a response to Upton Sinclair's The Jungle, an exposé of the Chicago meat packing industry, as well as other Progressive Era muckraking publications. While Sinclair's account focused on poor working conditions, the public was more alarmed by the risk of consuming bad meat. The book's claims were confirmed by the Neill-Reynolds report, commissioned by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1906. Roosevelt, skeptical of Sinclair's socialist views, sent labor commissioner Charles P. Neill and social worker James Bronson Reynolds to conduct surprise visits to Chicago meat packing facilities. Despite the meat packers' efforts to conceal the inspection—working three shifts a day for three weeks—Neill and Reynolds were deeply disturbed by the unsanitary conditions and the lack of concern shown by plant managers, despite their limited field experience. Following their report, Roosevelt supported regulation of the meat packing industry and, on June 30, 1906, signed the Meat Inspection Act of 1906. The FMIA required USDA inspection of meat processing plants operating across state lines. On the same day, June 30, 1906, the Pure Food and Drug Act was enacted, granting the government broad jurisdiction over food in interstate commerce. The four primary requirements of the FMIA were established in 1906. After 1906, numerous additional laws were passed to further standardize the meat industry and its inspection. In 2012, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in National Meat Assn. v. Harris that the FMIA preempts a California law regulating the treatment of non-ambulatory livestock. Chronological legislation relative to U.S. Congressional revisions concerning the Federal Meat Inspection Act is also documented.
